name: self serving bias
definition: A cognitive or perceptual process that is distorted by the need to maintain and enhance one's self esteem.
example: If I do well on the exam, it's because of my academic prowess and hard work. If I do poorly, it's because the course was poorly taught, and the exam was poorly proctored.

name: accident (fallacy)
definition: an informal fallacy and a deductively valid but unsound argument occurring in a statistical syllogism (an argument based on a generalization) when an exception to a rule of thumb is ignored.
example: Cutting people with knives is a crime. Surgeons cut people with knives. Surgeons are criminals.

name: complex question (loaded question with implicit assumption)
definition: A question that is loaded with an implicit assumption.
example: 'Why are you lying to me?' is a question that presupposes you are lying to me. Any answer you give will force you to agree you are lying.

name: red herring
definition: Introducing irrelevant points to detract attention from a question.
example: A member of the press asks the president why they voted to expand a welfare program. The president responds, 'The strength of America is the strength of its communities, and I am proud to make our communities better places.'

name: metaphor
definition: a figure of speech that, for rhetorical effect, directly refers to one thing by mentioning another.
example: 'All the world's a stage, And all the men and women merely players' is a metaphor because it's a comparison without using 'like' or 'as.'

name: spatial reasoning
definition: The capacity to reason about the spatial relationships between objects.
example: The key fit into the box. Using spatial reasoning, one can deduce that the width of the key was smaller than the width of the box.

name: modus ponens
definition: A syllogism that is of the form 'If P then Q. P. Hence Q.'
example: 'If today is Tuesday, then John will go to work. Today is Tuesday. Therefore, John will go to work.'

name: statistical syllogism
definition: A syllogism that argues, using inductive reasoning, from a generalization true for the most part to a particular case.
example: 'Almost all people are taller than 26 inches. Gareth is a person. Therefore, Gareth is taller than 26 inches.'

name: emotional self regulation
definition: a complex process that involves initiating, inhibiting, or modulating one's state or behavior in a given situation.
example: Examples of emotional self regulation include meditating, pausing to collect oneself before speaking, and practicing stress management.

name: folk physics (common knowledge physics)
definition: The untrained human perception of basic physical phenomena.
example: 'If I roll the pen off of the table, it will fall to the floor.'

name: modus tollens
definition: A valid argument form: from a conditional P→Q and the negation of Q, infer the negation of P. The contrapositive of modus ponens.
example: A botanist states: 'If a sample is from genus Quercus, it has lobed leaves.' A new sample lacks any lobed leaves. By modus tollens, the sample is not from Quercus.

name: hypothetical syllogism
definition: A valid argument form: from P→Q and Q→R, infer P→R. Chains conditional statements transitively to license a longer-range inference.
example: If a tree is a Quercus alba, then it has lobed leaves; if it has lobed leaves, then it sheds in autumn. By hypothetical syllogism, if a tree is a Quercus alba, then it sheds in autumn.

name: disjunctive syllogism
definition: A valid argument form: from a disjunction P∨Q and the negation of one disjunct ~P, infer the remaining disjunct Q. Requires the disjunction to be exhaustive.
example: A clinician reasons: the patient's pneumonia is either bacterial or viral. The blood culture and procalcitonin rule out bacterial. By disjunctive syllogism, the pneumonia is viral.

name: contrapositive
definition: The transformation of a conditional P→Q into its logically equivalent form ~Q→~P. A statement and its contrapositive have identical truth conditions and license the same inferences.
example: The rule 'if a permit is approved, the applicant has paid the fee' has contrapositive 'if the applicant has not paid the fee, the permit is not approved.' Either form supports denying a permit when the fee is unpaid.

name: ad hominem
definition: An informal fallacy in which an argument is rebutted by attacking the character, motive, or attribute of the arguer rather than the substance of the argument itself.
example: A senator counters a colleague's deficit analysis by saying 'of course you'd say that — your district benefits from defense contracts.' The substantive numerical claims are not engaged with at all.

name: straw man
definition: An informal fallacy in which an opponent's position is misrepresented in a weaker, easier-to-refute form, and the weakened version is then attacked as if it were the original.
example: A scientist argues that a specific pesticide regulation is overly broad. A critic responds: 'so you want to let companies poison the water supply?' — substituting an extreme position for the actual nuanced one.

name: false dilemma
definition: An informal fallacy in which only two options are presented as if they exhaust the alternatives, when in fact additional or intermediate options exist; also called a false dichotomy.
example: A speaker insists 'either we ban gas-powered cars by 2030 or we accept catastrophic warming' — ignoring intermediate paths like phased transitions, hybrid adoption, or sectoral reductions.

name: slippery slope
definition: An informal fallacy in which a chain of escalating consequences is asserted to follow from an initial action without adequate evidence that each step in the chain would actually occur.
example: A debater claims that allowing same-day voter registration 'will lead to non-citizen voting, then to large-scale election fraud, then to the collapse of representative government' — without evidence linking each transition.

name: confirmation bias
definition: A cognitive bias in which one selectively notices, interprets, or recalls evidence consistent with a prior belief while underweighting or ignoring evidence that disconfirms it.
example: A manager who already believes a team member is unmotivated notices every late arrival and missed email, but does not notice the same patterns in other team members or the prompt follow-up the team member sent.

name: anchoring bias
definition: A cognitive bias in which an initial reference value disproportionately influences subsequent numerical judgments, even when the anchor is arbitrary or irrelevant to the quantity being judged.
example: A negotiator opens with $100,000. The counterparty's eventual offer of $80,000 feels like a major concession, even though the fair market value is closer to $50,000 — the opening anchor pulled the final number upward.

name: tu quoque
definition: An informal fallacy in which a person's argument is rebutted by accusing them of inconsistency or hypocrisy, rather than addressing the substance of the argument. Latin for 'you also.'
example: A doctor advises a patient to quit smoking. The patient retorts: 'You're a smoker yourself, so your advice doesn't count.' The medical claim about lung damage is unrelated to whether the doctor follows their own advice.

name: equivocation
definition: An informal fallacy in which a word or phrase shifts meaning between premises of an argument, making the conclusion appear to follow when it does not.
example: A customer argues: 'The bank's sign says "free checking," so the bank should not charge me for this cashier's check.' The word 'checking' shifts from 'checking account services' to 'any item containing the word check.'

name: appeal to authority
definition: An informal fallacy in which the testimony of an unqualified or out-of-domain authority is invoked to support a claim. Legitimate appeals to qualified expertise within an authority's actual domain are not fallacious.
example: A nutrition advocacy site argues that a high-dose vitamin regimen is safe because a Nobel laureate in physics endorsed it. The laureate's expertise does not extend to nutrition, so the endorsement provides no substantive support for the safety claim.

name: appeal to emotion
definition: An informal fallacy in which an argument relies on provoking pity, fear, anger, or other emotional responses in place of providing evidence relevant to the claim.
example: A defense attorney shows the jury photographs of the defendant's young children at home, rather than addressing the forensic evidence linking the defendant to the crime scene. The emotional appeal does not bear on the question of guilt.

name: post hoc ergo propter hoc
definition: An informal fallacy in which one event is asserted to have caused another simply because the first preceded the second in time. Latin for 'after this, therefore because of this.'
example: A city's crime rate dropped the year after a new mayor took office. A columnist credits the mayor's policies, ignoring that a federally funded community policing program launched in three high-crime precincts the same year.

name: circular reasoning
definition: An informal fallacy in which the conclusion of an argument is included, explicitly or implicitly, among its premises. Also called begging the question.
example: A reviewer argues a textbook is reliable because the author is a respected expert; when asked why the author is respected, the reviewer cites their reliable books. The argument never establishes external grounds for either claim.

name: hasty generalization
definition: An informal fallacy in which a broad conclusion is drawn from a sample that is too small, biased, or otherwise unrepresentative to support the inference.
example: A traveler visits Paris for three days, has two rude interactions with waiters, and concludes Parisians are unfriendly. Two encounters cannot ground a population-level claim about a city of two million people.

name: base rate neglect
definition: A cognitive bias in which prior probability information (the base rate of an event in the population) is ignored or underweighted in favor of specific case information, producing systematically wrong probability judgments.
example: A screening test for a rare disease is 99% accurate. A patient tests positive. Without considering that the disease only affects 1 in 10,000 people, an analyst concludes the patient likely has it — ignoring that most positives in this low-prevalence setting are false positives.

name: availability heuristic
definition: A cognitive shortcut in which the frequency or likelihood of an event is judged by how easily examples come to mind, leading to overestimation of vivid, recent, or memorable events relative to their actual base rates.
example: After watching repeated news coverage of shark attacks, a vacationer estimates ocean swimming is far riskier than driving the highway to reach the beach. The actual base rates are reversed by orders of magnitude.

name: sunk cost fallacy
definition: A cognitive bias in which past investments of money, time, or effort are used to justify continued investment in a course of action that no longer has positive expected value, ignoring that sunk costs are unrecoverable regardless of the decision.
example: A studio has spent $40 million on a film and the rough cut tests poorly. The executives approve another $20 million on reshoots, citing the existing investment, even though analysts project the recut version will still lose money.

name: abductive reasoning
definition: A form of inference that selects the hypothesis most likely to explain a set of observations, even when the hypothesis cannot be deductively proven from the observations. Also called inference to the best explanation.
example: A mechanic finds the engine misfires under load, the spark plugs are fouled, and the air filter is clean. A failing fuel injector best accounts for all three observations together. The mechanic abductively concludes the injector is the root cause and tests it first.

name: transitive inference
definition: A deductive operation in which an ordering relation that holds between A and B and between B and C is used to conclude the same relation holds between A and C, given the relation is transitive (e.g., taller-than, older-than, before).
example: A historian notes Manuscript A predates Manuscript B (carbon dating) and Manuscript B predates Manuscript C (a recorded transcription event). By transitive inference, Manuscript A predates Manuscript C, even without direct comparison.

name: necessary and sufficient conditions
definition: A distinction in conditional logic. A necessary condition for X is something without which X cannot occur; a sufficient condition is something that, if present, guarantees X. The two are independent — a condition can be necessary without being sufficient, sufficient without being necessary, both, or neither.
example: In a graduate program, attending all lectures may be necessary to pass (you cannot pass without it) but not sufficient (you must also pass the exam). Identifying which kind of condition a rule states determines what counter-example refutes it.

name: enumerative induction
definition: A form of inductive reasoning in which a generalization about a population is supported by observations of a sample of its members. The strength of the inference depends on sample size, representativeness, and the absence of disconfirming cases.
example: A field biologist examines 200 individuals of a newly classified bird species across three breeding sites and finds all are diurnal. By enumerative induction, she tentatively generalizes that the species is diurnal, pending observations from additional populations.

name: analogical inference
definition: A form of reasoning in which a property known to hold of one case is transferred to a similar case based on relevant similarities. The strength of the inference depends on which similarities are relevant to the property in question, not surface similarity alone.
example: A toxicologist knows compound A causes liver damage in rats and shares the same molecular core and metabolic pathway as compound B. By analogical inference, she hypothesizes B may cause similar damage and prioritizes targeted testing.

name: counterfactual reasoning
definition: A form of reasoning that considers what would have been the case if some past event had been different, holding the rest of the world fixed except for the consequences of the alternative event.
example: An accident investigator asks: would the collision have occurred if the brake light had been functional? Holding driver behavior, road conditions, and following distance fixed, the answer informs whether the malfunction was a but-for cause.

name: regression to the mean
definition: A statistical phenomenon in which extreme observations tend to be followed by less extreme ones, because the original measurement included a temporary unusual component. Misattributing this rebound to an intervention is a common error.
example: A school identifies the lowest-scoring 10% of students and gives them tutoring. On the next test, those students score higher on average. Some improvement may be from tutoring, but much would have occurred anyway — extreme low scores tend to drift upward toward the mean.

name: gambler's fallacy
definition: A cognitive bias in which past outcomes of an independent random process are believed to influence future outcomes — for example, believing that a streak of one outcome makes the opposite outcome more likely on the next trial, when the trials are in fact independent.
example: A roulette table has shown red on the last seven spins. A bettor reasons that black is 'due' and bets heavily on it. The wheel has no memory; each spin remains 18/38 for either color regardless of history.

name: framing effect
definition: A cognitive bias in which logically equivalent presentations of the same information lead to different judgments or decisions, depending on whether information is framed in terms of gains or losses, percentages or absolute numbers, and so on.
example: A treatment described as having '90% survival' is preferred more often than the same treatment described as having '10% mortality,' even by the same patients. The underlying probabilities are identical; only the frame differs.

name: hindsight bias
definition: A cognitive bias in which, after an outcome becomes known, people overestimate how predictable that outcome was beforehand. Often expressed as 'I knew it all along.'
example: After a startup fails, commentators describe the warning signs as obvious — crowded niche, inexperienced founder, short runway. Before the failure, those same signs were equally consistent with eventual success and were not flagged by the same commentators.

name: multi step word problem
definition: A numerical reasoning task that requires identifying multiple intermediate quantities, deciding which arithmetic operations connect them, and combining them into a final answer.
example: A bus has 24 seats. 14 passengers board at stop 1, 7 leave and 9 board at stop 2, and at stop 3 half of those onboard exit. How many remain? Answer: (14 - 7 + 9) / 2 = 8.

name: fraction percentage conversion
definition: Converting between fractions, decimals, and percentages, and applying the conversion to compute a quantity.
example: If a price drops from $80 to $60, the discount is 20/80 = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%.

name: unit conversion
definition: Translating a measurement from one unit system to another by applying conversion factors, including chained conversions.
example: A car traveling 90 km/h covers 90,000 m in 3,600 s, i.e. 25 m/s.

name: synonym selection in context
definition: Choosing among candidate synonyms the one that best matches a target word's meaning given its surrounding sentence, accounting for register and connotation.
example: In 'her terse reply ended the meeting', the best synonym for 'terse' is 'curt', not 'silent' or 'rude'.

name: word meaning from context
definition: Inferring the meaning of an unfamiliar or polysemous word from the surrounding sentence and broader passage cues, without external lookup.
example: 'The lawyer's peroration moved several jurors to tears' — peroration here means the closing emotional summation of a speech, inferred from 'lawyer' and 'moved jurors to tears'.

name: subject verb agreement
definition: Identifying when a verb's number does not match its grammatical subject, particularly across intervening phrases that obscure the subject.
example: 'The list of items, including several rare books, are on the desk' — error: 'list' is singular, so the verb should be 'is'.

name: dangling modifier
definition: Identifying when a participial or descriptive phrase at the start of a sentence has no logical subject in the main clause, producing an absurd reading.
example: 'Walking through the park, the cherry blossoms were stunning' — dangling: the cherry blossoms aren't walking; rewrite as 'Walking through the park, I found the cherry blossoms stunning.'

name: key point extraction
definition: Identifying the main claim or argument of a passage and distinguishing it from supporting evidence, qualifications, or peripheral remarks.
example: Passage about a study showing exercise reduces anxiety, with caveats on sample size and confounders. Key point: 'Exercise was associated with reduced anxiety in this sample, though the authors caution that the small N and lack of randomization limit causal claims.'

name: agent identification
definition: Determining the entity that performs the action expressed by a verb in a sentence, distinguishing it from patients, instruments, and beneficiaries — including in passive constructions.
example: 'The trophy was awarded to Maria by the committee' — agent: 'the committee'; patient: 'the trophy'; beneficiary: 'Maria'.

name: verb tense identification
definition: Naming the tense, aspect, and voice of a finite verb form in a sentence, including compound forms like past perfect progressive or future passive.
example: 'The contract had been being negotiated for months' — past perfect progressive passive.

name: proportional reasoning
definition: Setting up and solving a proportion to compute an unknown quantity from a given ratio, including rate problems, scaling, and density-style mappings.
example: If 3 machines produce 240 widgets in 8 hours, then 5 machines (same rate) produce 240 / (3 × 8) × 5 × 8 = 400 widgets in 8 hours.

name: antonym recognition
definition: Selecting the word that most directly opposes the meaning of a target word in a given context, distinguishing true antonyms from related-but-not-opposite terms.
example: In 'his prodigal spending alarmed the family', the antonym of 'prodigal' is 'frugal' (not 'generous' or 'careful').

name: polysemy disambiguation
definition: Determining which of a word's multiple established senses is intended in a particular sentence, using surrounding lexical and semantic context.
example: 'The bank approved the loan after reviewing the statements' — 'bank' here is the financial institution sense, not the riverbank sense, signaled by 'approved', 'loan', 'statements'.

name: parallelism violation
definition: Identifying items in a list or series that do not share the same grammatical form (mixing nouns with gerunds, infinitives with finite verbs, etc.) and proposing a parallel revision.
example: 'She likes hiking, to swim, and biked on weekends' — violates parallelism; corrected: 'She likes hiking, swimming, and biking.'

name: tense consistency
definition: Detecting unjustified tense shifts across clauses or sentences within a passage, distinguishing them from intentional shifts that reflect a temporal change.
example: 'The detective entered the room and notices a faint smell of bleach' — unjustified shift from past to present; corrected: '...entered... and noticed...'.

name: one sentence summary
definition: Producing a single sentence that captures the central claim or main event of a passage, constrained to omit supporting detail and qualifications while remaining accurate.
example: Passage: a 600-word account of how a city introduced congestion pricing, including history, opposition, and revenue figures. Summary: 'The city implemented congestion pricing in 2024, generating $480M in its first year while drawing organized opposition from outer-borough commuters.'

name: topic sentence identification
definition: Locating the sentence within a paragraph that states the paragraph's main idea, distinguishing it from supporting evidence, transitions, and asides.
example: In a paragraph that opens with 'Ocean acidification poses an existential threat to coral reefs.' followed by four sentences of pH data and reef-decline figures, the first sentence is the topic sentence.

name: argument structure mapping
definition: Identifying the premises, intermediate conclusions, and final conclusion of an argument in a passage, distinguishing claims from rhetorical framing.
example: 'Since vaccinated employees rarely require hospitalization (premise 1), and the office insurer charges 30% more for unvaccinated staff (premise 2), our HR policy should require proof of vaccination (conclusion).'

name: patient identification
definition: Identifying the entity that undergoes or is affected by the action expressed by a verb, distinguishing it from agents, instruments, and beneficiaries — particularly across passive and dative constructions.
example: 'The contract was signed by the partners with a fountain pen' — patient: 'the contract'; agent: 'the partners'; instrument: 'a fountain pen'.

name: voice classification
definition: Classifying a clause as active, passive, or middle voice based on the syntactic relationship between subject and verb, including identifying agent demotion in passives and reflexive constructions.
example: 'The package was delivered yesterday' — passive (subject is patient; agent is omitted/optional). 'The window broke during the storm' — middle (no overt agent; verb is intransitive use of a transitive root).
